Public Liaison Committee-Ottawa Valley Waste Management Board   
 
 
As required by the Ottawa Valley Waste Recovery Centre’s Ministry of Environment 
Environmental Compliance Approval and the Partners’ Inter-Municipal Agreement: 
 
 
7.8 The elected Council of each of the parties shall appoint a representative on a public liaison 
committee (the “PLC”). 
 
The primary function of the PLC will be to liaise with the ratepayers within partner 
Municipalities (Town of Petawawa, City of Pembroke, Township of Laurentian Valley and the 
Township of North Algona Wilberforce) and the Ottawa Valley Waste Management Board 
concerning OVWRC operations. 
  
The Committee will facilitate communication of information, ideas, concerns, issues and 
technology through interfacing with the public, government agencies, the business community 
and related organizations and individuals so as to promote, publicize and improve the waste 
management system.    
 
The committee will elect a Chair at the beginning of each term which coincides with the four 
year term of elected Council.  Each meeting must have a minimum of 51% of the PLC 
representatives to have a quorum. 
 
PLC members missing more than three consecutive meetings per year may be subject to removal 
from the committee. 
 
The PLC will generally meet quarterly or at the call of the Chair. The meetings will be held at 
the Centre.  The Chair or designate will attend OVWMB meetings to report on PLC activities.    
 
Minutes shall be prepared by the Centre’s Communications Officer and will be included in the 
OVWMB meeting agenda.   
 
As a minimum, the following items of discussion shall appear on each agenda: 
i) Review of Minutes from last meeting 
ii) Public Concerns: reports of any questions or concerns that were received  
iii) Update on Operations: report from staff regarding changes to programs or operations 
that the PLC should be aware of.  
iv) Discussion and review of Communication items: OVWRC staff will present 
communication items for PLC input. 
 
Each PLC member or alternate PLC member shall receive a per diem of $75 per meeting based 
on meeting attendance.  

 
 
 
ROLES AND RESPONSIBILITIES: 
PLC  
The PLC will adopt the following roles and responsibilities:  
a) Educate themselves and stay current with Ottawa Valley Waste Recovery Centre 
 
operations. 
b) Communicate with the ratepayers through various community outreach events (Open 
Houses, Home shows, Presentations, etc.);  
c) Provide comments and feedback to Ottawa Valley Waste Management Board;  
d) Provide comment on public consultation processes (i.e. ECA changes, Zoning Changes, 
By-Laws, etc.);  
e) Provide comments on Public Communications (i.e. newsletters, newspaper 
advertisements, collection schedules, etc.);    
f) Be accessible to ratepayers through phone or written contact;   
g) Accept resident’s written comments and present these comments to the Ottawa Valley 
Waste Management Board or Ottawa Valley Waste Recovery Centre staff; and  
h) Report to the Board on PLC activities at monthly Board meetings via written or  
 
verbal presentations.  
 
 
OVWRC Staff 
 
The OVWRC staff will adopt the following roles and responsibilities:  
 
a) Provide accurate and up to date information to the PLC in order for the PLC to offer  
information/guidance to the ratepayers;  
b) Promote the PLC committee as a contact (through verbal notification at public events and 
newspaper ads).

Inaugural Council Meeting Marks Beginning of 2026–2030 Council Term
-
Nov 19, 2026
All News
Community Updates
Council & Public Notices
Press Releases
The Town of Plympton-Wyoming officially welcomed its new term of Council during the Inaugural Council Meeting held on November 18, 2026.
During the ceremony, members of Council took their Oath of Office, formally beginning their service to the residents of Plympton-Wyoming for the 2026–2030 term.
The evening brought together Council members, staff, family, and community supporters to recognize this important milestone and the responsibilities that come with serving the community. It also provided an opportunity to reflect on the priorities and opportunities that lie ahead for the municipality.
The Town congratulates Mayor Gary Atkinson and all members of Council as they begin this new term and looks forward to working together to continue building a strong and vibrant community for residents, businesses, and visitors alike.

Dear Emergency Management Partners, 
  
Today, our government introduced the Emergency Management Modernization Act that, if 
passed, would modernize the Emergency Management and Civil Protection Act (EMCPA).  
 
The EMCPA and its regulations have not been comprehensively updated in more than 15 
years. Since then, the nature of emergencies has changed. The rising frequency of extreme 
weather events and the threat of cyber-attacks on Ontario’s digital infrastructure mean that 
we must ensure our emergency management framework reflects today’s realities.  
 
If passed, these amendments to the EMCPA would strengthen provincial leadership and 
coordination of emergency management by facilitating Emergency Management Ontario as 
the one window for coordinating provincial emergency management activities. Additionally, 
the proposed legislation would enhance community capacity in emergency management. 
This includes clarifying the process for municipalities to declare local emergencies and 
granting municipalities the authority to plan for and respond to emergencies based on their 
unique needs and capacity. 
 
The proposed amendments, if passed, would strengthen planning and coordination with 
emergency management partners, including by outlining the ability to enter into agreements 
and liaise with public and private sector partners, including municipalities, Indigenous 
communities, and other governments. In addition, the proposed amendments would enable 
future emergency management program and plan requirements to be established for 
designated entities that provide or operate critical infrastructure, subject to further 
engagement with partners, to support continuity of services and operations.  
 
Over the summer, Emergency Management Ontario engaged with more than 480 partners 
to inform proposed amendments, including municipalities, First Nations communities, and 
emergency management organizations. We look forward to further collaboration with our 
partners as we build a stronger, more resilient province, capable of ensuring the safety and 
wellbeing of communities across Ontario. The proposed amendments are posted on 
Ontario’s Regulatory Registry and Environmental Registry for your review and feedback.  
 
On behalf of Premier Ford and the Government of Ontario, thank you for your continued 
partnership in emergency management.

Election Day is Monday, October 26, 2026!
Community Strength Shines Through After Fire 
at Kawartha Home Hardware in Lakefield
In October 2025, the community of 
Lakefield came together in the face 
of an unexpected and difficult event 
when a fire broke out at Kawartha 
Home Hardware. While the incident 
resulted in significant disruption for 
the business, displaced residents 
and surrounding area, what stood 
out most in the days and weeks that 
followed was not the damage itself, 
but the strength, compassion, and 
resilience of the community.
Almost immediately, residents, local 
business owners, and neighbouring 
communities began to respond. 
Messages of support spread quickly, 
with many sharing memories of the 
store as more than just a hardware 
retailer, but as a long-standing 
community hub where neighbours 
ran into one another, advice was 
freely given, and projects of all 
sizes were supported. The fire was 
not only a loss of a building, but it 
was also felt as a loss of a familiar 
gathering place.
In the aftermath, local businesses 
and community organizations 
stepped forward to help fill gaps, 
offering supplies, temporary support, 
and even space for coordination as 
recovery efforts began. What might 
have been a moment of isolation 
instead became a clear example of 
mutual aid and shared responsibility.
Residents, too, played a vital role. 
Many expressed patience and 
understanding as services were 
disrupted, while others offered 
practical help or simply checked in 
on staff and owners to show support.
As recovery efforts moved forward, 
the focus gradually shifted from 
immediate disruption to rebuilding 
and renewal. While the process 
takes time, there has been a shared 
sense of optimism that the business 
will return stronger, supported by a 
community that values it.
The fire is a reminder of what 
community resilience looks like in 
practice.

Summer, 2026
As we come into the final year of our Council’s term, 
we are going through a significant change to our 
senior team. With the retirements of the CAO, Fire 
Chief, Treasurer & Clerk over the next nine months, 
maintaining positive momentum in project workplans 
will be challenging. With the need to focus internally 
on recruitment for these key positions in our senior 
management team, staff will need to maintain a focus 
as new leadership is onboarded. During my second term 
on Council from 1996 to 2000, Smith and Ennismore 
were merged and then, late in the term, Lakefield 
was amalgamated to create the Township of Smith-
Ennismore-Lakefield. The current senior leadership 
team mostly came from the previous amalgamated 
townships and through promotion, became the strong 
team we have today. Returning to Council in 2022 as 
Deputy Mayor, it was comforting to see these familiar 
faces leading Selwyn Township. I wish Janice, Gord, Lane 
and Angela all the best in their retirement.
As one of the Selwyn Township appointed 
representatives to the Otonabee Region Conservation 
Authority (ORCA), along with Lakefield Councillor 
John Boyko, we have been busy working through the 
changes to provincial legislation that will merge 36 
conservation authorities into 9 regional authorities by 
2027. There are still several governance issues that need 
to be resolved but future local board representation 
will come from the upper tiers like Peterborough 
County and not Township appointments. The current 
ORCA Board of Directors will continue beyond their 
traditional municipal term ending in October into 2027 
to complete the transition to the new regional Board of 
Directors.
With the dissolution of the former regional corporation 
Peterborough Kawartha Economic Development (PKED) 
in late 2024, Peterborough County assumed the primary 
responsibility for economic development and tourism 
across Peterborough County. The new team will take the 
lead in rebranding the region as “The Kawarthas” and 
provide marketing leadership to local businesses and 
tourism operators. Branded as “The Local Advantage” 
where business finds balance is supported by the 
Growth Resilience Opportunity & Workforce (GROW) 
Economic Development Plan. The Plan will support 
existing businesses, sector growth in agriculture, 
tourism and small manufacturing, lead local economic 
development efforts, create investment readiness and 
celebrate local successes.
Ron Black, Selwyn Deputy Mayor
It has been another busy year for Selwyn, with 
continued investment and growth across the Township. 
In Bridgenorth, development applications have been 
submitted for 38 new residential units, each situated 
on 0.65-acre lots behind the Home Hardware plaza. 
An additional application proposes three residential 
buildings, each containing three units, on the 8th Line; 
both developments will be privately serviced. Site plan 
applications have also been submitted for the first phase 
of Lakefield South, where 34 condo townhouses are 
proposed to replace the originally planned four apartment 
buildings, which would have totalled 110 units.
The Township has applied for funding through the 
Home Energy Retrofit Program in hopes of establishing 
a program that would support homeowners in making 
energy-efficient upgrades such as converting to heat 
pumps, improving insulation, upgrading doors and 
windows, and enhancing lighting and other home 
systems. Stay tuned for updates as more information 
becomes available.
With our ReLeaf program, we work with our community to 
restore and enhance the Township’s tree canopy. This past 
year we distributed 600 trees to private property owners. 
This helped replenish the trees lost from the 2022 Derecho 
and the 2025 Ice storm.
During Local Government Week 2025, I visited with 
students at St. Paul’s, Lakefield Public School, Chemong 
Public School and St. Martins. The students were all very 
engaged and a plethora of ideas were shared.
Selwyn Public Library has developed a new Strategic 
Plan, available on the website www.mypubliclibrary.ca. If 
you are looking to better connect with our community, I 
invite you to volunteer at one of our branches. It can be a 
rewarding experience.
It is with sadness that we say goodbye to our Smith-
Ennismore Community Policing volunteers, who were 
housed on Ward Street. Over the years, Anita and Val 
provided excellent leadership to all our dedicated 
volunteers who helped support programs such as Lock 
it or Lose it, Boat Safety, Car Seat programs, and speed 
enforcement, to name a few. The OPP will continue to use 
the space on Ward Street. 
Speaking of Ward Street, the detailed design plans are 
60% completed by the County and will be done by this 
summer. The project will involve significant work with 
partners such as Hydro for some utility relocation.
Peterborough County was proud to announce the release 
of its G.R.O.W. Economic Development plan, its first 
economic development plan to foster Growth, Resilience, 
Opportunity and Workforce development across the 
Region. The County launched its first interactive tourism 
map which can be viewed at thekawarthas.ca
Enjoy the seasons in Selwyn and all we have to offer. 
Remember, I am just a phone call away.

As part of the Joint Accessibility Advisory Committee, 
I help provide information and recommendations to 
Selwyn Township and Peterborough County to improve 
accessibility. My role has provided many collaborative 
opportunities, including Sharing Our Stories Sessions at 
Trent University and the Ontario Public Service.
Selwyn communities are fortunate to have many caring 
residents and community groups, including Julie Grant, 
Nancy Turner and the Ennismore Optimist Club who 
brought the inclusive playground to Ennismore. I have 
partnered with Julie, Nancy, members of the Joint 
Accessibility Advisory Committee and community 
members to develop mini videos about accessibility. The 
goal is to educate; we hope to present our successes at 
the 2026 AMO Conference to inspire other communities.
This year, Kawartha Land Trust joined the Peterborough 
County Geographic Information System (GIS) 
Department, Selwyn Township staff, and Trent 
University’s School of Environment for the Accessible 
Trails Project. Working with Trent student Ashlyn Harper, 
we collected additional data to support individuals with 
different abilities to traverse the Ennismore Heritage Trail.
Special thank you to Selwyn Township and Selwyn Public 
Library staff who secured funding to expand seniors 
programming. However, this funding is temporary. I’m 
seeking other opportunities to keep these programs 
running beyond 2026.
For the 2026 AMO Conference, I have requested a 
delegation with the province to reinstate support for the 
Reduced Impaired Driving Everywhere (RIDE) program. 
With the province rolling back funding, local community 
groups and the municipality must make up the deficit or 
not run the programs. These programs help keep Selwyn 
communities safe.
In 2025, Council supported a one-year ice allocation pilot. 
I am extremely thankful to the user groups and Selwyn 
Township staff who supported engaging dialogue to 
ensure feedback was received and built into the reports 
for Council’s consideration. These efforts set us up for 
success, especially in Ennismore where we all look 
forward to enjoying the refurbished arena floor.
The Ennismore Curling Club has also undergone 
renovations. To support the Club’s fundraising efforts, 
brainstorming is underway. Stay tuned for upcoming 
events to engage with and support the Club!
Thank you to all the sponsors, vendors, volunteers and 
committee members Londa Junkin, Vince Young, Richard 
Northey, Amy Stevenson and Mike Richardson who made 
the 2025 Shamrock Festival a great success.
Finally, special thank you to Cathy Young, Mary-Claire 
Moher and the Ennismore Heritage Days committee 
– the celebration of the 200 Anniversary of the Peter 
Robinson Settlers was unforgettable.

Change is a natural part of every healthy organization, 
and from my perspective as a member of Council, it also 
represents an opportunity to strengthen leadership, renew 
priorities, and prepare our municipality for the future. As 
our Township moves through 2026, we are experiencing an 
important leadership transition during an election year.
Several respected senior staff members are preparing 
for retirement after years of dedicated service to our 
community. Their professionalism, experience, and 
commitment to public service have helped guide Council, 
support municipal operations, and advance projects that 
benefit residents. On behalf of Council and the community, 
I want to sincerely thank them for their contributions and 
leadership over the years.
At the same time, we are welcoming a new Chief 
Administrative Officer who will play an important role 
in shaping the next chapter of our organization. As 
additional leadership transitions occur over the coming 
months, the CAO will help build and strengthen the senior 
management team to ensure the Township continues to 
operate effectively and respond to the evolving needs of 
residents.
Leadership transitions can create uncertainty, but they 
also create opportunity. They allow municipalities to 
bring in fresh perspectives, modern ideas, and renewed 
energy while continuing to build on the strong foundation 
already in place. Council’s role throughout this process 
is to provide stability, support collaboration, and ensure 
residents continue to receive accountable and effective 
municipal services.
This transition also serves as a reminder that municipalities 
are always evolving. Councils change, staff change, 
priorities shift, and communities continue to grow. What 
remains constant is the shared responsibility to serve 
residents with professionalism, transparency, and care.
Looking ahead, I remain optimistic about the future of 
our Township. We are fortunate to have dedicated staff, 
engaged residents, strong community organizations, and 
volunteers who care deeply about this community. While 
change can bring challenges, it also creates opportunities 
for growth, innovation, and renewed focus.
From my seat in Council Chambers, these transitions 
represent an opportunity to strengthen our organization, 
support new leadership, and continue building a resilient 
and forward-looking municipality for years to come.

Municipal governance is about teamwork. To serve the 
people of Selwyn, Council and senior staff coordinate with 
the County, OPP, Peterborough Police, and agencies and 
companies that provide services as well as the provincial 
and federal governments. It’s also about balancing 
priorities because there’s not the time, staff, or money to do 
everything we’d like, all at once. Plus, stuff happens, like a 
derecho or an ice storm, or, like last winter, more snow than 
anticipated. The teams pivot.
Selwyn residents helped create the Township’s Strategic 
Plan. It and other plans guide the creation of the Township’s 
annual budget and the workplans of senior managers. 
The budget this year is about $26 million. Less than half 
comes from property taxes. The rest is derived mostly from 
fees, investment income, and the provincial and federal 
governments.
This year, the Township budgeted and planned for an 
ambitious program to advance our plans and improve our 
community. They include the replacement of the 54-year-old 
Ennismore arena floor. At the Ennismore Waterfront Park, 
the trails will be improved through signage and boardwalk 
repairs. Due to the amazing initiative of Julie Grant that 
gathered wide support and generous donations, we will see 
the construction of a fully accessible playground. 
Meanwhile, the Township has assumed management of the 
Lakefield Campground and the Lakefield-Smith Community 
Centre has had its Olympia ice machine replaced.
The Fire Department will replace one of its aging pumpers 
and some of its old personal protective equipment that 
protects firefighters from heat, flames, and hazardous 
materials. To meet provincial legislation requiring firefighters 
to meet new certification standards, the part time training 
position will be changed to full time.
Portions of Woodland Drive and Fallis Drive will be micro-
surfaced. Work will improve Templetiny Crescent and Kinsale 
Road. The Lakefield Water and Sewer budget and a large 
provincial grant will allow the 69-year-old old water and 
sewer pipes beneath part of George Street to be replaced 
and the street brought to urban standard. Surfacing 
work will improve Mudd Road, Centre Line, Gannon Line, 
Birchbend Road, Ennis Road, and Holden Road. New parking 
areas will be added near the Lakefield pickleball courts.
Meanwhile, services from snow removal to by-law 
enforcement will continue. Taken together, the projects and 
services will contribute to ensuring that Selwyn remains a 
great place to live, work, invest, and visit.

The Township of Selwyn launched

private properties following significant 
damage from the March 2025 ice 
storm. The program was supported 
through Hydro One Networks Inc.’s 
Ice Storm 2025 Recovery Grant and 
built on the success of the Township’s 
previous ReLeaf programs.

native trees were made available to 
residents at no cost. Species included 
Red Oak, Swamp Oak, Sugar Maple, 
Silver Maple, and Red Maple. These 
trees were selected for their suitability 
to Ontario’s climate, their ability 
to support biodiversity, and their 
resilience to severe weather conditions.
By supporting private property 
plantings, the initiative contributed 
to broader community-wide efforts to 
restore green spaces, improve climate 
resilience, and enhance the local 
landscape.

Whereas pursuant to Section 238 of the Municipal Act, 2001, as amended, every 
municipality and local board shall pass a procedure By-law for governing the calling, place 
and proceedings of meetings; 
 
Now Therefore the Council of the Corporation of the Township of Selwyn Enacts as 
follows; 
 
Definitions 
 
1. 
In this By-law: 
 
a) 
“Abstain” means a member who is lawfully entitled to vote but chooses not to 
exercise their right to vote on a matter, and in such cases in abstention shall be 
deemed as a negative vote (Municipal Act S. 246. (2)). 
 
b) 
“Clerk” means the Clerk of the Corporation of the Township of Selwyn. 
 
c) 
“Committee” means any advisory or other Committee, subcommittee or similar 
entity of which at least 50 per cent of the members are also members of one or 
more councils or local boards.  A local board does not include police services 
boards or public library boards (Municipal Act S. 238. (1)). 
 
d) 
“Council” means the Council of the Corporation of the Township of Selwyn. 
 
e) 
“Electronic Participation” includes telephone, video, audio or audio-visual conferencing, 
or any other interactive method whereby Members, staff and the public are able to hear 
the Member(s) participating by electronic means and the Member(s) participating by 
electronic means are able to hear other Members, staff and the public. 
 
f) 
“Head of Council” means the Mayor of the Corporation of the Township of Selwyn. 
 
g) 
“Live streaming” is a method of providing video over the internet in real time. The 
video stream can be saved and archived allowing those with internet access the 
ability to view recordings at their convenience. 
 
h) 
“Meeting” means any regular, special, committee or other meeting of a Council, or 
of a local board or of a committee of either of them, where, 
 
(a) a quorum of members is present, and  
(b) members discuss or otherwise deal with any matter in a way that materially 
advanced the business or decision-making of the Council, local board or Committee 
(Municipal Act S. 238 (1). 
 
i) 
“Pecuniary Interest” means a direct or indirect pecuniary interest of a member of 
Council within the meaning of the Municipal Conflict of Interest Act, R.S.O. 1990, as 
amended. 
 
j) 
“Presiding Officer” means the member of Council who, as determined under Section 
12, 13 or 17 of this By-law, is responsible to preside over or act as the Chairperson 
of a meeting.

k) 
“Point of Order” means an issue or concern regarding conformity to this By-law

Public or Civic Holidays 
 
6. 
When the day for a regular meeting of the Council is a public or civic holiday, the 
Council shall meet at the same hour on the following day, which is not a public or 
civic holiday, unless an alternative day is determined by resolution of Council. 
 
Cancelling and Rescheduling Meetings 
 
7. 
Council may, by resolution passed at a regular meeting, cancel a scheduled regular 
meeting or reschedule a regular meeting to another date and may hold a meeting at 
another location other than the Council Chambers. 
 
In the event of an exceptional circumstance (e.g. emergency situation, unsafe 
weather or where the Clerk becomes aware that quorum will not be met) the Clerk 
can cancel a scheduled meeting and seek input from the members on an alternate 
date/time, if required. The Clerk shall notify Council members of the cancellation 
and any other relevant parties as soon as possible and post notice of the 
cancellation on the Township’s website.  
 
Where quorum can be met, the Clerk can conduct the meeting by Electronic 
Participation or a combination of in-person and Electronic Participation. In the event 
that the format of the meeting is changed to Electronic Participation or a 
combination of in-person and Electronic Participation, the Clerk shall notify the 
members of Council of the format and any other relevant parties as soon as 
possible and post the change on the Township’s website.  
 
Special Meetings 
 
8. 
The Head of Council may at any time summon a special meeting of Council on 
forty-eight (48) hours notice to the members of Council, or upon receipt of the 
petition of the majority of the Members of the Council, the Clerk shall summon a 
special meeting for the purpose and at the time mentioned in the petition.   
 (Municipal Act S.240 ) 
 
9. 
Forty-eight (48) hours notice of all special meetings of Council shall be given to the 
Members, either verbally or written, through the Clerk’s Office. 
 
10. 
The only business to be dealt with at a special meeting is that which is listed in the 
notice of meeting. 
 
11. 
In the event of an emergency, as determined by the Head of Council, a meeting 
may be called at any time.

absent through illness, or refuses to act or that office is vacant, the Deputy Mayor

so acting as the Presiding Officer shall have all the rights, powers and authority of

Presiding Officer

The Head of Council, except where otherwise provided, shall preside at all meetings 
of Council. (Municipal Act S.241(1))

Calling of Meeting to Order and Quorum 
 
15. 
A majority of the whole number of members required to constitute a Council is 
necessary to form a quorum.  (Municipal Act S.237(1)) 
 
16. 
As soon after the hour fixed for the holding of the meeting of the Council as a 
quorum is present, the Head of Council shall take the Chair and call the meeting to 
order. 
 
Absence of Presiding Officer 
 
17. 
Should the Head of Council not attend within five (5) minutes after the time 
appointed for a meeting of Council and the Acting Head of Council is not present to 
assume the role of Presiding Officer, the Clerk shall call the members to order and a 
Presiding Officer shall be appointed by resolution from among the members 
present, and they shall preside until the arrival of the Head of Council or the Acting 
Head of Council and while so presiding shall have all the powers of the Head of 
Council.  (Municipal Act S.242) 
 
 
No Quorum 
 
18. 
If no quorum is present fifteen (15) minutes after the time appointed for a meeting of 
the Council, the Clerk shall record the names of the members present and the 
meeting shall stand adjourned until the date of the next regular meeting.  The 
members present shall be entitled to remuneration as approved from time to time. 
 
Curfew 
 
19. 
Council meetings  
 
No item of business, with the exception of the confirming By-law and a motion to 
adjourn, may be dealt with at a Council meeting after 4:00 pm unless the time for

such case, the extension shall provide for an additional thirty (30) minutes to deal 
with the business of Council, i.e. the meeting shall be extended to 4:30 pm. Any 
further extension of curfew shall require a resolution of Council passed 
unanimously.

MEETING TYPE: Regular Council Meeting
To:
Council
From:
Jackie Trenholm, Deputy Clerk
 Date:
April 16, 2025
 Subject:
2026 Municipal Election Matters
 Report No.:
2025-529
TITLE: 2026 Municipal Election Matters
RECOMMENDATION:
THAT Council authorizes the passing of By-law No. 25-25, Being a By-law Relating to 2026
Municipal Election Matters (language(s) to be used for election forms/notices/information; use
of alternative voting method; use of vote-counting equipment).
PURPOSE:
The purpose of this recommendation is to enable Council to make certain decisions respecting
the 2026 Municipal Election, including the use of the "telephone/internet" voting method.
BACKGROUND:
Several items must be addressed relative to the 2026 Municipal Election, including:
1.    Use of Alternative Voting Methods
2.    Advance Poll
3.    Early Voting and/or Reduced Voting Hours
4.    Use of vote-counting equipment
5.    Language(s) in Notices/Forms/Information
6.    Payment of rebate for campaign contributions
7.    Ward(s) review/changes
8.    Electronic filing of financial statements
9.    Submitting a By-law or question to the electors (question on the ballot)
10.  Appointment of Compliance Committee
DISCUSSION:
Item No. 1: Use of Alternative Voting Methods

The Municipality had been employing the vote-by-mail (VBM) voting method for several prior
general municipal elections (2003, 2006, 2010 and 2014). This alternative voting method has
been successful, having yielded higher voter turnout rates over traditional elections in each of
the last four general elections.
While this method has increased voter turnout, compared to the traditional in-person polls, the
participation rate has decreased over the last decade-and-a-half, as follows:
•    Voter turnout 2003 – 60.61%
•    Voter turnout 2006 – 57.72%
•    Voter turnout 2010 – 56.86%
•    Voter turnout 2014 – 55.95%
Given this gradual, but steady, decline in voter participation, staff recommended the use of the
telephone/internet voting method in the 2018 general election, the 2020 by-election and the
2022 general election. Voter turnout for those elections was as follows:
•    2018 General Election –     55.21% 
•    2020 By-election –    32.48%
•    2022 General Election -  33.10%
Given the trend in municipal elections, across Ontario, of having fewer voters participate in
such elections, achieving a 55.21% voter turnout in 2018 was excellent, and placed Sioux
Lookout in among the highest of voter turnout results in Ontario. By-elections typically result in
lower number of voters. The 2020 By-election turnout was approximately 2.5% higher than the
last by-election in 2015. The 2022 voter turnout was lower than the 2018 general election.
When there isn’t a mayoral race, voter turnout is typically lower.
Vote-by-Mail versus Telephone/Internet Voting – An Analysis
Election Principles
Despite which voting method is selected, it is the responsibility of the Clerk/Returning Officer
to uphold the following election principles:
•    The secrecy and confidentiality of the individual votes is paramount;
•    The election must be fair and non-biased;
•    The election must be accessible to all voters;
•    The integrity of the process must be maintained throughout the election;
•    There must be certainty that the results of the election reflect the votes cast; and
•    All voters and candidates must be treated fairly and consistently. 
Vote by Mail – Overview
Electors receive a voting kit in the mail. They mail in their signed declaration form along with
their secrecy envelope containing their marked ballot. The declaration form is scanned prior to
voting day; the secrecy ballot is kept in a secure ballot box until the close of election. On
Election Day, Staff open the ballot boxes containing the secrecy envelopes and review each
ballot to determine if the ballot is spoiled or rejected. Staff then feed the ballots through a vote
tabulating machine or count them manually. Once all of the ballots have been fed through the
vote tabulator (or counted manually), the tabulator totals the votes and provides a printable
receipt of the results to election officials, or the totals of votes cast and counted manually are

reported to the Returning Officer.
Advantages and Disadvantages: Vote-by-mail (VBM)
Advantages:
Signed  declaration  –  provides  security against voter fraud
Improved size and efficiency. Desk top tabulators are hooked up to a PC laptop and can
scan 40 ballots per minute and results are quick. They also store the image of each
ballot for recount/audit purposes.
Longer voting period
Disadvantages:
With VBM, staff are required to facilitate vote tabulation by feeding ballots into vote
tabulators, or physically/manually examining each ballot, and must make a determination
with respect to spoiled and rejected ballots
Staff resources and time - secrecy ballot envelopes cannot be opened until close of
voting. Ballots must then be organized, reviewed, scanned, counted and then eventually
destroyed.
If not using vote-counting equipment, manual vote-counting is extremely time consuming
– unofficial results in 2014 were not available until 2:00 a.m. (6 hours after close of
voting).
Opportunity for Spoiled ballots – vote does not count (e.g. elector included ballot with
signed declaration card; no signed declaration form or no declaration form included;
marking on the ballot that does not indicate choice or there is no marking on ballot)
Spoiled ballots – the voter has no way of knowing if their ballot was spoiled. There is no
confirmation process.
Potential to receive voter kits by unintended recipient which includes the ballot
Postal service – takes five days for voter to receive vote by mail kit; takes five days for
municipal office to receive marked ballot with secrecy envelope (total 5-10 days) by mail,
unless dropped off at municipal office
Costs – more expensive voting method due to need for more staff; manual count;
training of staff, etc.
Internet/Telephone Voting - Overview
Internet Voting – Electors receive a Voter Information Letter containing a Personal
Identification Number (PIN) in the mail. They log onto the election server on any computer,
vote by using their keyboard in response to a virtual ballot, the vote is stored on the election
software. The elector receives confirmation of their vote by way of a confirmation number or
printable receipt. At the close of Election Day, the internet software totals the votes received
and provides a printable receipt of the results to election officials.
Telephone Voting – Electors receive a Voter Information Letter containing a Personal
Identification Number (PIN) in the mail. They call a toll-free number from a touchtone phone;
vote by pressing buttons in response to a voice recording and the vote is stored by the
election software. The elector receives confirmation of their vote by way of a confirmation
number. At the close of Election Day, the telephone voting results are combined with the
internet voting results for one total result. A printable receipt of the results is made available to
election officials.

It is recommended that both internet and telephone options be provided to electors for the
2026 municipal election.
Advantages and Disadvantages of Internet/Telephone Voting
Advantages:
Less staff and administrative resources required and less expensive overall (except in
first year of implementation, due to public education costs)
No ballot errors/spoiled ballots because the software does not permit it. There are built in
reminders or safeguards to prevent accidental voting
Voter is provided with confirmation that their vote counted by issuance or confirmation of
a receipt
Elector participation is real time and results are immediate
Ballot destruction after election is electronically completed and verified
Voter has the opportunity to review selection and make changes prior to submitting vote
Lowered carbon footprint; environmentally sustainable due to less paper required
Recounts are instantaneous and inexpensive
Most accessible form of voting. Allows persons with disabilities the opportunity to
completely mark their ballot in private without the assistance of a designated friend or
election official, therefore providing greater dignity
Disadvantages:
Not everyone has access to a computer or is computer literate; however, telephone
voting would be the alternative to those who do not have internet access or low levels of
computer literacy
Security and viruses; voter authentication - however, the preferred vendor has
implemented robust measures to mitigate such threats
Telephone voting takes time – audio ballot
Telephone voting - Voter cannot see the names of the candidates
Other Benefits of Internet/telephone Voting
•    provides convenience, accommodates changing lifestyles, demanding work schedules;
•    enhances accessibility for students studying away from home, those travelling, shift
workers, infirmed persons, and persons with language barriers.
•    for persons with disabilities, it provides greater dignity and privacy for electors;
•    engages a wider range of age demographics, provides greater accuracy and fast results, is
convenient for seasonal residents, and has the potential for increased voter turnout.
Public Education & Outreach
Public education and outreach will play a critical role in the 2026 municipal election, should the
telephone/internet voting method be adopted. Although this method has been used several
times in Sioux Lookout, to ensure that concerns and questions regarding this voting method
are adequately addressed, a prior election education campaigns will be enhanced and
administered by the Clerk.
In order to mitigate concerns regarding accessibility for senior citizens to vote, the Clerk, as in
the 2018, 2020 and 2022 elections, will arrange to attend multi-residential senior complexes
throughout the community to provide senior citizens the opportunity to vote at their residence.
Additionally, for those who are not comfortable with internet voting or telephone voting on their
own, an electronic voting station will be established at the Municipal Office, with staff on hand

to provide assistance, as requested. Furthermore, remote voting locations will be established
at the Sioux Lookout Senior’s Centre, the Sioux Lookout Meno Ya Win Health Centre, the
William George Extended Care Unit, the Nishnawbe-Gamik Friendship Centre, and in Hudson.
Accessibility for Persons with Disabilities
Internet/Telephone voting offers the most accessible form of voting.  Voters are offered the
greatest secrecy and less assisted voting thereby enhancing the quality of the vote and
anonymity.
Security
Section 89 of the Municipal Elections Act provides for penalties for any contravention of the
Act, as follows:
A person is guilty of an offence if he or she,
(a)    votes without being entitled to do so;
(b)    votes more times than this Act allows;
(c)    votes in a voting place in which he or she is not entitled to vote;
(d)    induces or procures a person to vote when that person is not entitled to do so;
(e)    having appointed a voting proxy that remains in force, votes otherwise than by the proxy;
(f)    having been appointed a voting proxy, votes under the authority of the proxy when the
elector has cancelled the proxy, is no longer entitled to vote or has died;
(g)   before or during an election, publishes a false statement of a candidate’s withdrawal;
(h)   furnishes false or misleading information to a person whom this Act authorizes to obtain
information;
(i)    without authority, supplies a ballot to anyone;
(j)    delivers to the deputy returning officer to be placed in a ballot box a paper other than the
ballot the deputy returning officer gave him or her;
(k)    takes a ballot away from the voting place;
(l)    at an election, takes, opens or otherwise deals with a ballot, a ballot box, or a book or
package of ballots without having authority to do so;
(m)  attempts to do something described in clauses (a) to (l)
Clearly, accountability of voting rests with the voter and there are penalties associated with
voter fraud. Unsupervised voting facilitates the potentiality of these offences. Voter
impersonation, coercion and fraud are concerns which are mitigated through the design of any
voting system, regardless of whether it is a supervised or unsupervised model.
Item No. 2: Advance Poll
The use of the vote-by-mail or telephone/internet voting methods eliminates the need for
advance polls. Additionally, determination of this matter has now been delegated to the Clerk,
via the Municipal Elections Act, Council no longer makes these decisions.
Item No. 3: Early Voting and/or Reduced Voting Hours
The vote-by-mail voting or telephone/internet voting methods eliminates the need for these
measures. Additionally, determination of this matter has now been delegated to the Clerk, via
the Municipal Elections Act, Council no longer makes these decisions.
Item No. 4: Use of Vote-Counting Equipment

The Municipality had used Electronic Vote Tabulators (EVTs) in the 2000, 2003, 2006 and
2010 Municipal Elections. Ballots were created and coded by Ward, School Board
candidate(s) and Municipal Council (Mayor and Councillors-at-Large) candidates and
processed by the EVT on voting day. In the past, this has resulted in election results within
minutes of the close of polls.
For the 2014 Municipal Election, the Clerk chose to use manual vote-counting procedures
given that vote-counting equipment rental had significantly increased in cost increase since
the 2010 Municipal Election. The primary impact on the election was a longer time-frame
between the close of polls and the announcement of the unofficial results – a total of six hours.
If Council chooses to use the Vote-by-Mail voting method in 2026, vote tabulators will be
required to ensure the efficient tabulation of results; this is an additional cost to using this
voting method.
Item No. 5: Language(s) in Notices/Forms/Information
Prescribed forms (those set by legislation) must be provided in English only, but may be
provided in English and French only. Other forms/notices/information can be provided in
English, French or any other language, providing Council passes a by-law permitting such.
In one previous election, prior to 2003, some of the Notices were provided in both English and
Oji-Cree. This exercise was costly and was subsequently discontinued. It should be noted that
the onus is on the elector to provide translation services when voting. In 2003, 2006 and 2010,
the Clerk recommended and Council passed a By-law to provide notices in Oji-Cree at the
discretion of the Clerk.
Staff recommends that Council permit notices to be published in Oji-Cree for the 2026
Municipal Election, at the discretion of the Clerk.
Item No. 6: Payment of Rebate for Campaign Contributions
Council may pass a by-law for the payment of rebates to persons who make contributions to
candidates running for Council. The payment of these funds come from general Municipal
funds (i.e., from the Sioux Lookout taxpayer). There is significant work involved in setting-up
and administering this process. Seasoned Municipal practitioners recommend against this
practice.
Staff recommends that Council not implement a system for rebates for campaign
contributions.
Item No.7: Ward(s) Review/Changes
On September 19, 2012, Council passed By-law No. 50-12, Being a By-law to Restructure the
Ward System in the Municipality of Sioux Lookout. This By-law eliminated Ward 2 (Sioux
Lookout). The effect of this change was that in the 2014 Municipal Election, the number of
"Councillors-at-Large" to be elected increased from four to five, in addition to the Ward 1
(Hudson) Councillor and the Mayor.
Council had expressed interest in reviewing the remaining Ward (Ward 1, Hudson) to
determine the value in retaining it as Sioux Lookout’s only Ward. The Clerk presented Council

with the results of the 2021 Ward Boundary Review and recommended the elimination of the
sole remaining Ward (Ward 1 (Hudson). Council passed By-law No. 103-21 Being a By-law to
Dissolve Ward 1 (Hudson), the only remaining ward within the Municipality of Sioux Lookout,
effective for the 2022 general Municipal Election.
As such, there is no longer a requirement for a Ward Boundary Review.
Item No. 8: Electronic Filing of Financial Statements
Prior to recent changes to the Municipal Elections Act, Sec. 78 (7) empowered the council of a
local municipality to pass a by-law to authorize the filing of financial statements in an electronic
format. This matter has now been delegated to the Clerk.
To facilitate the timely submission of Financial Statements, and in recognition of the trends
towards the increasing use of electronic measures/systems, the Clerk intends to provide for
this type of filing. Traditional "hard copy" filing of Financial Statements may be accepted.
Item No. 9: Submitting a By-law or Question to the Electors
This matter will be dealt with in a separate Report, closer to the deadline for making such a
decision (i.e., March 1, 2026). 
Item No. 10: Appointment of Compliance Audit Committee
The appointment of a Compliance Audit Committee is a requirement under the Municipal
Elections Act (Sec. 88.37 (1)). This matter will be dealt with in a separate report to be brought
before Council prior to October 1, 2026.
RELATIONSHIP TO THE STRATEGIC PLAN:
This is a routine administrative matter with no direct link to Council’s Strategic Plan.
FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS:
The estimated cost for Vote-by-Mail for the 2026 municipal election is $52,890.
The estimated cost for telephone/internet voting for the 2026 municipal election is $26,700.
Staff highly recommends not using both the telephone/internet and vote-by-mail options.
Investigation into this matter revealed that this dual-method option is undesirable for the
following reasons:
•    Significantly higher costs
•    Confusion for electors
•    Greater challenges in administering the election
•    Greater chance for voter fraud
Council, as per previous elections, has been setting aside money in the Elections Reserve

since 2019 to ensure there are sufficient funds available for the 2026 election, and to save
having to budget for the entire election amount in 2026.

WHEREAS the Municipality of St.-Charles has identified the revitalization and increased utilization of the St.-Charles Arena as a strategic priority;
AND WHEREAS the Municipality's 2025–2035 Community Strategic Plan identifies opportunities to enhance arena utilization, develop multi-season recreation programming, upgrade and add multi-use courts, relocate and upgrade community facilities, increase year-round programming, and promote cultural activities;
AND WHEREAS the St.-Charles Arena currently operates primarily as a single ice-pad facility and has significant potential to serve the community through expanded year-round recreational, cultural, social and community programming;
AND WHEREAS recent community consultation and the Municipality's review of the future of the delivery of municipal services have identified the need to consider the long-term use, accessibility, sustainability, and utilization of municipal community facilities;
AND WHEREAS the Municipality is undertaking consideration of the future use of the Arena and recognizes the opportunity to create a centralized, multi-use community facility capable of supporting recreation, cultural activities, community meetings, programming, events, and other community services;
AND WHEREAS the Arena is located in an area that is anticipated to benefit from additional residential development and will be located adjacent to a new licensed child-care facility, providing an opportunity to create a community hub serving existing and future residents;
AND WHEREAS Council recognizes that external funding opportunities may be available to assist with the capital costs associated with the modernization, accessibility improvements, energy efficiency, building improvements, equipment, and conversion of the Arena;
BE IT RESOLVED THAT Council for the Corporation of the Municipality of St.-Charles hereby supports, the conversion and redevelopment of the St.-Charles Arena into a multi-use and cultural community hub consistent with the objectives identified in the Municipality's 2025–2035 Community Strategic Plan;
AND BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT Council supports the Municipality pursuing and submitting applications to applicable federal, provincial, and other funding programs to assist with the conversion of the St.-Charles Arena into a multi-use and cultural community hub;
AND BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT municipal staff are directed to identify and pursue appropriate funding opportunities and to prepare and submit applications where the proposed project meets the eligibility requirements of the applicable funding program;
AND BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT any municipal contribution, borrowing, construction commitment or significant capital expenditure required to proceed with the project beyond approved funding and existing Council-authorized expenditures shall be brought back to Council for consideration and approval;
AND BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT the Chief Administrative Officer, or designate, is authorized to execute funding applications and related administrative documents on behalf of the Municipality where permitted under the Municipality's policies and applicable legislation.

Welcome to the Township of Tay's Meeting Portal. We pride ourselves on being accountable, transparent, and accessible. Through this Portal, you will be able to view agendas, reports, minutes, and by-laws, subscribe to updates, and search documents.
 Meeting Transparency 
Please be advised that all regular and special meetings of Council are held in-person in Council Chambers at the Municipal Building located at 450 Park Street, Victoria Harbour, while all Committee of the Whole meetings are held virtually. All Council and Committee of the Whole meetings are live streamed and will be available on the Tay Township YouTube Channel. Questions about the live stream or meetings should be directed to clerk@tay.ca.
 Strong Mayor Powers
Effective May 1, 2025, the Mayor of Tay Township has Strong Mayor Powers. The Mayor is required to exercise these powers in writing, give notice to the Municipal Clerk, and make decisions and directives available to the public, subject to the Municipal Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act.  Mayoral decisions and directives are available on the Township’s webpage: Strong Mayor Powers
 Delegation Requests
Interested in providing a delegation to Council? Please fill out the Delegation Request Form and submit to the Municipal Clerk at clerk@tay.ca or in-person at the Municipal Building. Approved delegations will be allowed ten (10) minutes to present in front of Council or Committee of the Whole, with additional time provided for questions by members of Council. Delegations will not be scheduled if the matter has already been before Council and a decision has been rendered. Further, multiple or repeat delegations on the same matter will not be scheduled unless new information on the matter is provided. Please Note: information provided on the Delegation Request Form will become part of the public record and be added to the public Council meeting Agenda.

City Council meets regularly to discuss and make decisions on matters affecting the community.
Regular Council meetings are usually held on the third Tuesday of each month at 6:00 p.m. These meetings are live-streamed on the City’s Facebook and YouTube channels, allowing residents to watch from home.
Committee of the Whole meetings are generally held on the first Tuesday of each month at 3:00 p.m.

 7.1
Cory Holmes - Stoco
 Local resident, Cory Holmes, will attend the Council meeting as a delegation to present information and a request to forming a “new stoco hamlet committee”.

Mr. Holmes will also request Council’s permission to use a space outside of the closed arena building on the parks and recreation land area to put a small to medium sized outdoor rink this winter (similar to what Marlbank recreation arena is already doing) to be organized by volunteers and not the Municipality Parks & Recreation department. 

Mr. Holmes will further outline a request for a new “stoco area recreation arena" task force be created. Where volunteers, community partners like the Lions Club, Kiwanis or small businesses can get involved with information sharing, community input and begin fundraising efforts to help with the municipality costs for repairs/changes to be made to the building.

 WHEREAS, the transportation of students to and from school is an essential public service that supports families, education, and the community; and
WHEREAS, many school bus drivers are employed on a part-time basis and are authorized by their employer to park their assigned mini or wheelchair-accessible school bus at their residence; and
WHEREAS, permitting these smaller school buses to be parked on private residential driveways can improve driver recruitment and retention, reduce unnecessary travel to and from bus yards, reduce fuel consumption and emissions, and improve operational efficiency; and
WHEREAS, mini and wheelchair-accessible school buses are generally between 19 and 25 feet in length and have a significantly smaller neighbourhood impact than full-size conventional school buses; and
WHEREAS, Section 3.9(5) of Parking By-law 89-2000 currently prohibits the parking of school buses, used as commercial vehicles and designed for carrying ten or more passengers, on private property in a residential zone, without distinguishing between mini and wheelchair-accessible school buses and full-size conventional school buses; and
WHEREAS, the proposed review seeks to balance the operational needs of school transportation providers with the preservation of the safety and character of residential neighbourhoods; and further
WHEREAS, this motion applies only to the parking of mini and wheelchair-accessible school buses on private residential driveways and does not propose permitting school buses to park on public streets.
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT Council directs staff to review Section 3.9(5) of Parking By-law 89-2000 and report back with recommendations regarding an amendment to permit mini school buses and wheelchair-accessible school buses not exceeding 26 feet (7.9 metres) in length to be parked on private residential driveways only, where the vehicle is assigned to a resident by a licensed school bus operator' and further
THAT staff consult with local school bus operators as part of the review and provide recommendations respecting appropriate eligibility requirements, safety considerations, operational conditions, and any other amendments necessary to implement such an exemption.  Ref. No. 26-22

  Should you wish to provide comments regarding a matter being considered below, please submit written correspondence and/or a Delegation Request Form.

To speak virtually during the Public Meetings, please submit a Delegation Request Form online to the Office of the Town Clerk by 8 a.m. on the day of the meeting. Those wishing to speak in-person are encouraged to submit a Delegation Request Form, but are not required to pre-register in order to speak at the Public Meetings.   Interested parties who wish to be notified of updates pertaining to a matter considered at a Public Meeting may submit an Interested Party List Registration Form. Town Staff will provide a brief overview of the application;

The Chair may call on the applicant and/or staff to provide clarification on matters raised by members of the public.

MEETINGS
Lanark County has a variety of committees that are working constantly to serve you better. Below is a description of each of our committees, as well as recent meetings that you can review. Click on the name of a specific meeting to review the details of that meeting.

HISTORY
As recently as 1997, Lanark County began operating in a two-tier system with sixteen local municipalities, 31 County Councilors, and nine standing committees. Commencing January 1, 1998, sixteen municipalities were restructured into eight municipalities, while County Council was reduced to sixteen members, and all County services were divided among the following four standing committees: Community Services, Corporate Services, Economic Development, and Public Works. Other Steering and Sub-Committees are available as support to the County.
 STRUCTURE
Council operates under a Committee of the Whole Structure, which consists of four committees; Community Services, Corporate Services, Economic Development and Public Works, whereby county council and committee meetings are generally held the second and fourth Wednesday of each month at 5pm.

PUBLIC DELEGATIONS
As per sub-section 9.4 of 2023-36 - Procedural By-Law:

Persons desiring to present information on matters of fact or make a request of Council shall give notice to the Clerk by submitting a written request, including the topics of conversation no later than 12:00 noon 9 days prior to the Meeting of Council or Committee.
 The Clerk has discretion to schedule Delegations at Meetings, subject to the volume of material on a given Regular Agenda, taking into account the following factors: order in which the requests were made; urgency of the request; subject matter relating to an agenda item; and frequency of delegations from the same individual/group.

Delegations shall be assigned by the Clerk to a Committee of the Whole agenda and only assigned to a Council agenda if time sensitive.
  Upon confirmation from the clerk, the delegate shall ensure that all material to be included in the agenda (presentation and background information) shall be submitted to the Clerk no later than seven (7) days prior to the Council meeting.
Delegations consisting of more than one person shall be limited to two speakers, being limited to no more than five minutes each.  The second speaker shall not repeat information provided by the previous speaker from that delegation and will be confined by the Chair to presenting new and/or additional information.
  The subject matter of a Delegation does not have to relate to a matter on the Agenda for that Meeting.
At the discretion of the Clerk, persons may generally only appear before Council or Committee once every six (6) months on different topics.
  No Delegate shall:
speak disrespectfully of any person;
use intemperate, course or abusive language or non-parliamentary language;
speak on any subject other than the subject for which they have received approval to address Council or a Committee;
disobey the rules of procedure or a decision of the Mayor or Chair; or
speak to Council about matters:
involving current or pending litigation;
involving insurance claims;
involving administrative complaints that have not been reported and investigated through processes established by bylaws, policies, procedures or protocols;
beyond the jurisdiction of Council; or
contrary to MFIPPA;
 Delegations who have previously appeared on the same subject matter, shall be limited to providing new information only in their subsequent appearance(s).
 For greater clarity, ‘new information’ shall constitute  substantive differences from original concepts, data, and/or themes presented at the initial delegation.
 Delegations are not permitted to address Committee on a policy matter upon which Council has already made a decision within the last 12 months, if it is in regard to a policy matter, or unless Council has decided to reconsider the matter.

If you require additional information, please contact the Clerk’s office at clerk@lanarkcounty.ca or at (613) 267-4200 ext. 1502

PUBLIC WORKS
The Public Works Department builds, operates, maintains and repairs the County road network consisting of 561 two-lane kilometres of roads and 1 four-lane kilometre of road and 77 bridge and culvert structures with spans greater than three metres. The Department also manages three patrol yards, three gravel pits, and two office buildings. The public works fleet includes approximately 40 vehicles including light and heavy trucks, heavy equipment, trailers and various tools and equipment. The Department is organized into four divisions:
• Operations
• Construction
• Administration
• Fleet and Equipment

BY-LAW NO. 7198-26 
OF 
THE CORPORATION OF THE COUNTY OF SIMCOE 
A By-law to Govern the Calling, Place and Proceedings 
of the Meetings of Council and Committees. 
Whereas Section 238(2) of the Municipal Act, 2001, S.O. 2001, c. 25 (“Municipal Act”), 
provides that every municipality shall pass a By-law governing the calling, place and 
proceedings of meetings; and  
Whereas by the adoption of Recommendation GOV-36-26, the Council of the County 
of Simcoe deems it expedient to enact a new updated Procedure By-law that reflects 
legislative requirements, to govern the calling, place and proceedings of the meetings 
of Council and Committees of the Corporation of the County of Simcoe;  
Now therefore, the Council of the Corporation of the County of Simcoe hereby enacts 
as follows:

 By-law No. 7198-26 
 
Page 3 of 56 
SHORT TITLE 
This By-law shall be cited as the Procedure By-law.  
PART 1 - GENERAL 
1.0 DEFINITIONS   
For the purpose of this By-law:  
 
"Business Sections" means the divisions within a regular Committee of the Whole 
meeting each dedicated to specific subject matters within the scope and responsibility of 
Council;  
 
"Business Section Chair" means the person appointed to preside during their 
respective section at a regular Committee of the Whole meeting;  
 
"Business Section Vice-Chair" means the person appointed who would preside over 
the proceedings of their respective section at a regular Committee of the Whole meeting 
in the absence of the Chair;  
 
"Chair" means the person appointed to preside at a meeting;  
 
"Chief Administrative Officer" means the Chief Administrative Officer of the 
Corporation of the County of Simcoe;  
 
"Clerk" means the County Clerk of the Corporation of the County of Simcoe or their 
designate; 
 
“Closed Session” means a meeting or a part of a meeting which is not open to the 
public in accordance with the Municipal Act;  
 
"Committee" means any Committee of Council or similar body of which at least 50 per 
cent of the members are also members of one or more councils or local boards, and 
includes the Committee of the Whole, Special or Ad Hoc Committees, Advisory 
Committees or a Task Force of Council;   
 
"Committee of the Whole" means all members of Council and appointed members 
sitting as a Committee for the purpose of conducting business in a less formal manner 
in accordance with this By-law;  
 
"Confirmatory By-law" means a By-law passed for the purpose of giving general effect 
to the decisions or proceedings of Council;  
 

 By-law No. 7198-26 
 
Page 4 of 56 
"Consent Items" means items placed in a section of the agenda that is used to adopt 
items with one motion. Consent items may be pulled from the list of consent items by 
any member, for further discussion, debate or motion;  
 
"Council" means the Council of the Corporation of the County of Simcoe;  
 
"Delegation" means an address to Council or a Committee at the request of a person 
or an organization wishing to speak;  
 
“Electronic Meeting” means a meeting held in whole or in part by videoconference, or 
other form of electronic means; 
 
"Head of Council" means the County Chair for the County of Simcoe or any member 
acting in the capacity of the County Chair;  
 
"Majority Vote" means an affirmative vote of more than one half of the members 
present and eligible to vote;  
 
"Meeting" means any regular, special, or other meeting of Council, or of a Local Board 
or a Committee of either of them where, a quorum is present and where members 
discuss or otherwise deal with any matter in a way that materially advances the 
business or decision-making of the Council, Local Board or Committee;  
 
"Member" means a member of Council, a member of Committee or an alternate 
member of Council appointed by a lower-tier municipality under Section 268 of the 
Municipal Act; 
 
"Motion" means a proposal by a member presented in a meeting, in accordance with 
the rules of procedure, to deal with a matter before Council or Committee;  
 
"Presentation" means an address to Council or Committee that has the consent of the 
County Chair or Chair and was arranged at the request of Council, Committee or staff, 
and may include the presenting of an award, certificate, cheque, etc.;  
 
"Quorum" means the number of members required to be present at a meeting to 
validate the transaction of business, that number being more than half of the members 
of the Council or Committee who are eligible to vote;  
 
"Recess" means a short intermission in meeting proceedings which does not close the 
meeting, and after which business will immediately be resumed at exactly the point in 
proceedings where it was stopped;  
 

 By-law No. 7198-26 
 
Page 5 of 56 
"Recorded Vote" means a written record of the name and vote of every member 
present, voting on any matter or question at a Council meeting;  
 
"Resolution" means the decision of Council on any motion;  
 
"Two-thirds Majority Vote" means an affirmative vote of at least two-thirds of the 
members present and eligible to vote at a meeting. Weighted vote shall not apply to 
decisions where this By-law requires a two-thirds majority vote;  
 
"Vice-Chair" means the person appointed who would preside over the proceedings of a 
Committee meeting in the absence of the Chair;  
 
"Weighted Vote" refers to a vote where the number of votes allocated to members of 
Council is prescribed by County By-law or applicable legislation and is a written record 
of the name and vote of every member present, voting on any matter or question. A 
weighted vote shall only occur in a meeting of Council upon request and must be 
requested only prior to a matter or question being put. 
2.0 APPLICATION/INTERPRETATION 
 
2.1 Application  
The rules of procedure contained in this By-law, or any standing or special rules of 
order adopted by the Corporation of the County of Simcoe shall be observed in all 
proceedings of Council and, with necessary modifications, its Committees and 
Boards. Failure to strictly adhere to the rules of procedure contained in this By-law 
shall not invalidate the action(s) of Council or a Committee acting in good faith.  
 
2.2 Statutes Affecting By-law  
Whenever any reference is made in this By-law to a statute of the Legislature of the 
Province of Ontario, such reference shall be deemed to include all subsequent 
amendments to such statute and all successor legislation to such statute.  
 
2.3 Matters Not Specifically Provided for in this By-law 
 
Matters not specifically provided for in this By-law shall be decided by the County 
Chair or Chair, in accordance with as far as practicable, parliamentary procedures as 
generally outlined in "Robert's Rules of Order''. The Clerk may be called upon to 
provide advice regarding procedural matters. Following receipt of any advice from 
the Clerk, the County Chair or Chair shall announce their ruling.  
 
2.4 Notice Required for Amendment or Repeal of By-law  
This By-law, or any part thereof, shall not be amended or repealed at any meeting of 
Council unless notice of the proposed amendment or repeal has been given at a 
previous meeting of Council. The requirement to give this notice shall not be waived.  

 By-law No. 7198-26 
 
Page 6 of 56 
2.5 Suspension of the Rules of this By-law  
Except for statutory provisions or unless otherwise provided for within this By-law, 
any provision of this By-law may be suspended in whole or in part by Council on 
obtaining not less than two-thirds majority vote and weighted vote shall not apply.  
 
2.6 Statutory Requirements  
Notwithstanding anything in this By-law, where Council or a Committee convenes for 
the purpose of holding a hearing as required by any statute or By-law, the provisions 
of the statute and the Statutory Powers Procedure Act, as applicable, shall govern 
the proceedings. If there is found to be any conflict between this By-law and any 
statute or By-law, the provisions of the statute or By-law shall prevail.   
 
2.7 Schedules  
 
Schedules to this By-law shall form part of this By-law.  
 
2.8 Severability  
If any section or part of this By-law is found by any court of competent jurisdiction to 
be invalid, such section or part shall be deemed to be severable and shall not affect 
the validity or enforceability of any other provisions of this By-law or the By-law as a 
whole. 
 
2.9 Strong Chair Powers  
 
Despite any section of this Procedure By-law, Part VI.1 of the Municipal Act, Special 
Powers and Duties of the Head of Council and any applicable regulations, shall 
prevail.    
PART 2 - DUTIES/RESPONSIBILITIES AND POWERS  
3.0 DUTIES AND RESPONSIBILITIES OF COUNCIL   
3.1 Role of Council  
In accordance with the Municipal Act, it is the role of Council:  
a) to represent the citizens of Simcoe County and to consider the well-being and 
interests of the County;  
b) to develop and evaluate the policies and programs of the County;  
c) to determine which services the County provides;  
d) to ensure that administrative policies, practices and procedures and controllership 
policies, practices and procedures are in place to implement the decisions of 
County Council;  
e) to ensure the accountability and transparency of the operations of the County, 
including the activities of the senior management of the County; and  
f) to maintain the financial integrity of the County; and  
g) to carry out the duties of the County Council under the Municipal Act or any other 
Act. 

 By-law No. 7198-26 
 
Page 7 of 56 
4.0 CONDUCT OF MEMBERS  
 
4.1 Respectful Conduct  
Members in attendance at meetings shall conduct themselves with decorum in 
accordance with the provisions of this By-law and in a manner that demonstrates 
professionalism and fosters respect and recognition for the formal nature of such 
proceedings.  
 
4.2 Right to Participate  
Members shall have the right to full participation in the proceedings of Council 
unless prohibited by law or as otherwise prescribed in this By-law.  
 
4.3 Restrictions  
 Unless otherwise prescribed in the Municipal Act, no member shall: 
a) be absent from the meetings of Council for three successive months without 
authorization by way of resolution of Council;  
b) speak disrespectfully of the Reigning Sovereign, or of any member of the Royal 
Family, the Governor General, the Lieutenant Governor of any Province, any 
member municipality, any other Council member or any official or employee of 
the County;  
c) use indecent, offensive or insulting language in or against Council or any 
member;  
d) engage in private conversation while in a Council meeting or use electronic 
devices including cellular phones, portable devices and computers for the 
purposes of facilitating or engaging in private discussion with regard to any 
matter on the agenda and/or any matter under debate at a meeting, except for 
the purpose of communicating a proposed motion to the Clerk;  
e) use electronic devices including cellular phones, portable devices and computers 
in a manner which interrupts or is disruptive to the proceedings of the Council;  
f) make noise or disturbance while a vote is being taken and until the result of the 
vote is announced;  
g) where a matter has been discussed in a meeting or part of a meeting closed to 
the public (closed session), and where the matter remains confidential, disclose 
the content of the matter or the substance of deliberations of the closed session; 
except to the extent that Council has previously released or disclosed the matter 
in public;  
h) criticize any decision of Council except for the purpose of moving a motion that 
the matter be reconsidered;  
i) disobey the rules of the Council or a decision of the County Chair or Council on 
questions of order or practice or the interpretation of the rules of Council;  
j) absent themselves from and during any meeting without notifying the County 
Chair or Clerk; 

 By-law No. 7198-26 
 
Page 8 of 56 
k) during any meeting, be dressed in a manner that is considered as unprofessional 
or which demonstrates a lack of due respect for the proceedings.   
4.4 Pregnancy and Parental Leave  
Notwithstanding Subsection 4.3 a), a member is permitted to take a leave in 
accordance with the rules of the County’s Pregnancy and Parental Leave for 
Members of Council policy.      
4.5 Improper Conduct - Order to Vacate  
A member may be required to vacate the meeting for a portion of, or for the balance 
of a meeting when, in the opinion of the Chair, a member is not conducting 
themselves in a proper manner and/or persists in breaching the rules of procedure. 
In such cases, the Chair, after three warnings, will order the member to vacate the 
meeting. Should the member refuse to leave the meeting, the Chair shall take the 
necessary action to expel the member. Should the member be requested to vacate 
the meeting, they shall do so immediately and such member forfeits their 
entitlement to compensation as provided under this By-law or the Council 
Remuneration By-law and policies of the County.  
 
4.6 Compliance with Policies and Code of Conduct  
All members shall adhere to this By-law and any other requirements related to 
conduct as may be contained within the Council Code of Conduct and any other 
County policies or By-laws adopted by Council. 
5.0 POWERS AND DUTIES OF COUNTY CHAIR AS HEAD OF COUNCIL  
 
Where applicable, the process for the appointment of County Chair shall be in 
accordance with Schedule 1 to this By-law.  
 
5.1 Statutory Duties  
In accordance with the Municipal Act, it is the role of the County Chair:  
a) to preside over meetings of County Council so that its business is carried out 
efficiently and effectively;  
b) to provide leadership to County Council;  
c)  without limiting clause b), to provide information and recommendations to County 
Council with respect to the role of Council described in Subsections 3.1 d) and e) 
of this By-law;  
d) to represent the County at official functions; and  
e) to carry out the duties of the Head of Council under the Municipal Act or any other 
Act.  
 
 

 By-law No. 7198-26 
 
Page 9 of 56 
As Chief Executive Officer, pursuant to Section 226.1 of the Municipal Act, the 
County Chair shall:  
a) uphold and promote the purposes of the County;  
b) promote public involvement in the County's activities;  
c)  act as the representative of the County both within and outside the County, and 
promote the County locally, nationally and internationally; and  
d) participate in and foster activities that enhance the economic, social and 
environmental well-being of the County and its residents.  
 
5.2 County Chair Presides at Meetings of Council  
The County Chair shall preside at all meetings of Council. 
 
5.3 Duties as Chair  
The Chair shall preside over meetings of Council in a manner that provides for 
business to be carried out efficiently and effectively and shall:  
a) open the meeting of Council by taking the position of Chair and calling the 
members to order; 
b) announce the business before the Council in the order in which it is to be acted 
upon and close the meeting when business has been concluded or recess the 
meeting as required;  
c) maintain order and preserve decorum during the meeting;  
d) receive, submit to a vote and announce the results of the vote for all motions, 
resolutions and By-laws presented;  
e) decline to put to a vote, motions which do not comply with the rules of procedure, 
or which are not within the jurisdiction of Council;  
f) rule on all procedural matters;  
g) expel or exclude from any meeting any person whom the Chair feels has 
exhibited improper conduct at the meeting;  
h) to authenticate by way of signature, as necessary, all direction, By-laws, and 
proceedings of Council;  
i) adjourn or suspend the meeting, without any motion being put, if they consider it 
necessary because of grave disorder. 
 
5.4 Absence of County Chair  
Should the County Chair not be in attendance at a Council meeting within fifteen 
(15) minutes of the time a quorum is present after the scheduled commencement 
time for a meeting of Council, or after resumption of the meeting after a recess, the 
Clerk shall call the Members to order and a Chair shall be chosen from amongst the 
Business Section Chairs (Committee of the Whole), as per the order below, and that 
individual shall preside until the arrival of the County Chair:

b) the Human Services Business Section Chair shall preside; in their absence;

5.5 County Chair Vacating the Chair  
The County Chair may designate any other member to preside over a portion of a 
Council meeting when they leave the Chair for any reason.  
 
5.6 Substitution - Powers  
Any member appointed to preside over a meeting shall have and may exercise all 
the rights, power, authority and is subject to the obligations of the Chair as it relates 
to the chairing of proceedings, and as provided for under this By-law. 
 
5.7 Ex-Officio Member - County Chair 
The County Chair shall be an ex-officio member of all Committees of Council by 
virtue of the office and when attending, shall have full voting privileges and shall be 
counted for the purposes of quorum.  
 
5.8 Official Representative of the County  
The County Chair will be expected at all times to maintain positive public relations in 
carrying out duties. The County Chair will be the official spokesperson for County 
Council and coordinate the presentation of the County's position to the public and to 
other external public bodies, agencies and organizations. The County Chair will be 
the official representative of County Council at all official functions to which the 
County may be invited. In the event that it becomes impossible for the County Chair 
to attend a function, the County Chair may appoint another member of Council to act 
as a delegate as may be appropriate.  
 
5.9 County Chair - Use of Vehicle  
While on County business, the County Chair shall have the use of a vehicle for 
which the County shall be responsible for all associated expenses.  
 
5.10 Report Improper Conduct  
It shall be the duty of the County Chair to report to Council through the appropriate 
Committee, the name of any Member of any Committee or Board who does not 
appear to be properly performing their obligations to the committee or board on 
which they were appointed.  
 
5.11 Vacancy - Office of the County Chair  
In the event the Office of the County Chair should become vacant, within the 
meaning of the Municipal Act, the vacancy shall be filled in accordance with the 
Municipal Act.

PART 3 - COUNCIL MEETINGS  
6.0 MEETINGS OF COUNCIL  
 
6.1 Location for Council Meetings  
Meetings of Council shall be held in the Council Chamber at the County of Simcoe 
Administration Centre, 1110 Highway 26, Midhurst or other such location which may 
be designated by the County Chair or Council from time to time or published on the 
agenda.  
 
6.2 Inaugural Meeting  
Unless provided otherwise in a meeting notice, the Inaugural Meeting of Council 
shall be held in-person at 1:00 p.m., on the second Tuesday in December following a 
regular municipal election. The Mid-term Inaugural Meeting shall be held in-person 
at 1:00 p.m. on the second Tuesday in December approximately halfway through a 
Council term, if required.  
 
6.2.1 Public Holiday  
In the event that the regularly scheduled day for the Inaugural falls on a public 
holiday, the Inaugural meeting shall be held at the same hour on the next day 
following that is not a public holiday.  
 
6.2.2 Inclement Weather or Emergency  
The Clerk, in consultation with the Chief Administrative Officer, may postpone 
the Inaugural Meeting if they are of the opinion that weather conditions and/or 
an emergency situation warrants such postponement for public safety or other 
similar reasons, and reschedule the meeting to the first suitable day following at 
the same hour.  
 
6.2.3 Notification of Postponement  
The Clerk shall inform the members elect prior to the scheduled time of 
postponed meeting and the alternate date of the meeting.  
 
6.2.4 Agenda/Proceedings  
The Clerk shall be responsible for the content of the agenda of Inaugural 
Meetings. Inaugural meetings of Council shall generally be for the purpose of 
introducing the County Chair and administering the Oaths of Office to Council.   
No other business other than what is stated on the Inaugural agenda shall be 
conducted.
